description.narrative: Although the Government of Rwanda (GoR) promotes civic participation in guiding frameworks, GoR leaders are not accustomed to meaningfully engaging citizens in prioritization, planning and assessment processes and tend to regard citizen participation forums as a place to tell and inform rather than to listen and respond to citizens. Additionally, while several policies and legal frameworks exist to address inequality and prevent discrimination, knowledge of these is lacking at decentralised levels and implementation is often poor, resulting in disparities in citizens’ access to their rights and appropriate services that will enable them to live in a more just and equal society. The proposed programme aims to see local and national government leaders purposefully consult their constituency to inform decisions, be responsive to citizens’ concerns, include a gender perspective in planning and budgeting and address the specific needs of vulnerable and marginalized groups. The specific outcomes are the following: - Civil Society partners are more effective in their work to influence and mobilize. This means that by the end of the programme PO's have been trained in policy analysis and organisational issues, that PO's have been supported on strategies and work to influence by alliances and that PO's have developed plans/strategies for improving influence and organisational strategies. - Citizens acted and participated in decision-making for their rights. This means that by the end of the programme citizens and duty bearers have knowledge about accessing their rights and responsibilities. Female community representatives have knowledge about policies, government programmes, law and rights. People have accessed support to resolve conflict and violation of rights. Decision-making foras have been facilitated. Professionals and para-professionals are enabled to provide assistance on conflict prevention and mediation practices and finally that women, men, girls and boys have knowledge on gender discrimination and how to prevent it. - Local and national government have formulated policies and plans that reflect the concerns raised by citizens and gender equality considerations. This means that by the end of the programme that decision-makers are informed and challenged on policy and service delivery issues, gender discrimination, and issues reported by citizens and vulnerable groups. Decision-makers’ and local leaders are capacitated by partners on citizen engagement, justice and equality. Decision-makers are also informed through documentation and research.

Norwegians Peoples Aid (NPA) and their programme Public Policy and Information, Monitoring and Advocacy (PPIMA) has been implemented in Rwanda since 2010 and unites 15 local partners in a unique collaboration to make citizens aware of their fundamental rights and provide them with the necessary skills to participate in positive actions to raise their views and interests with decision-makers and service providers.
The proposed PPIMA programme 2020-2024 intends to support CSOs and citizens to access their rights and participate in and influence the formulation and implementation of national and local policymaking, planning and governance. This is done by working with supporting civil society initiatives that are centered on: Civic participation and empowerment: Supporting citizens to raise and express their opinions and interests with decision-makers, to seek accountability and to advocate for local government planning and decision-making which is influenced by those citizens' concerns and gender equality considerations. Conflict resolution and supporting access to justice and rights: Supporting citizens’ knowledge of their rights and access to mechanisms for justice, reporting corruption and resolving conflict in the community, particularly as it relates to gender discrimination and GBV. Civil society influencing: Using research, media engagement and advocacy to influence debates and generate dialogue between citizens, CSOs and decision-makers.
PPIMA works at both the national and the district level, and in 2020 – 2024 will be operational in 16 of Rwanda’s 30 districts.

Norwegians Peoples Aid (NPA) och deras program Public Policy and Information, Monitoring and Advocacy (PPIMA) har implementerats i Rwanda sedan 2010 och förenar 15 lokala partners i ett unikt samarbete för att göra medborgarna medvetna om deras grundläggande rättigheter och öka deras kapacitet att föra fram sina åsikter och intressen till beslutsfattare och tjänsteleverantörer.
Det föreslagna PPIMA-programmet 2020-2024 avser att stödja civilsamhällesorganisationer (CSO: er) och medborgare att verka för ökad respekt för sina rättigheter samt att delta i och påverka utformningen och genomförandet av nationell och lokal politik, planering och styrning. Detta görs genom att stödja civilsamhällets initiativ som är inriktade på: - Medborgardeltagande och kapacitet: stödja medborgarna att ta fram och uttrycka sina åsikter och intressen mot beslutsfattare, ökat ansvarsutkrävande, förespråka lokal planering och beslutsfattande som påverkats av medborgarnas prioriteringar och jämställdhetsöverväganden. - Konfliktlösning och stöd för att ökad tillgång till rättssystemet och ökad respekt för rättigheter: Stödja medborgarnas kunskap om deras rättigheter och tillgång till mekanismer för rättvisa, rapportera korruption och lösa konflikter i samhället, särskilt när det gäller könsdiskriminering och könsbaserat våld. - Påverkansarbete av det civila samhället: Att använda forskning och medieengagemang för att påverka debatter och skapa dialog mellan medborgare, CSO och beslutsfattare.
PPIMA arbetar på både nationell- och distriktsnivå. År 2020 - 2024 kommer programmet att verka i 16 av Rwandas 30 distrikt.

The contribution has recently undergone two evaluations: one final evaluation and one outcome harvesting which identified both intended and unintended outcomes. In addition to this, the fourth phase of PPIMA was subject to a mid-term review in August 2022, to see that the programme was on the right track. PPIMA IV is similar to PPIMA III but has an additional focus on emerging issues such as environment and climate.
Sida provided 85.2 MSEK to PPIMA IV during the five years (2020-2024). Findings from the final evaluation and the outcome harvesting are summarised below.
Final evaluation
The evaluation found that PPIMA IV achieved significant milestones across all three outcomes. The programme built capacity of CSO partners, including their internal management systems (tools, policies and procedures). The evaluation points to the ability to conduct evidence-based advocacy work as one of the important skills acquired.
The evaluation was conducted in accordance with the OECD DAC criteria for evaluations. It was well-aligned to national priorities as decentralization is an explicit goal for Rwanda. The programme effectively reached its targets, it was coherent in that it built logically on previous PPIMA phases and related to existing initatives. The programme made efficient use of the budget and 98 % was spent. PPIMA contributed to a more empowered civil society and responsive governance structures which is evidence of its impact. The evaluation concludes that long-term sustainability of PPIMA's impact is promising as the results are expected to remain in terms of citizen participation through CSC as a formal mechanism supported by the government of Rwanda.
PPIMA's biggest achievement is undoubtedly the citizen scorecard process (CSC) which contributed to the empowerment of citizens and their opportunities to influence their own life. The evaluation found that citizens were empowered through the CSC to find solutions together with local decision makers to issues in areas such as infrastructure repair and social support initiatives. Citizens strengthened their capacity to participate in planning and budget processes, and decision makers changed their perception of citizens from be seen as some type of opposition, to an actor interested in community change for the benefit of everyone. The evaluation also points at the Governance Focal Person (GFP) and their role in promoting the citizens in these processes.
The evaluation confirms that PPIMA contributed to behavioural change in regards to gender sensitive policy making as citizens were empowered to voice their concerns and it resulted in improved gender budgeting and an amended GBV law.
The challenges brought up in the evaluation relates to the limited reach of the programme, given that only 19 out of 30 districts in Rwanda were included. The government has repeatedly asked NPA to extend the programme to all districts but there has not been funding for that. The lack of contingency funding was another problem which restricted NPA to respond to emerging issues such as when PPIMA got involved in public interest litigations which created new demands that could not be met. Another finding from the evaluation was that some targets were set too low, leading to significant gaps between projections and actual outcomes.
Outcome harvesting 2009-2024
The outcome harvesting collected outcomes from the whole PPIMA period, i.e. 2009-2024, both intended and unintended. The results resemble the final evaluation findings to a large extent. A few of the most tangible outcome harvests are listed below, clustered into four main outcome areas (which all relate to the three main objectives of the PPIMA programme).
Citizen Participation Empowerment
As a result of PPIMA, citizens and civil society organizations are effectively utilizing the Community Scorecard (CSC) to influence local government decisions and manage resources better. PPIMA partners facilitated the use of the CSC process in 16 out of 30 districts, helping to gather citizen priorities that informed the national budget and district plans. This led to significant policy changes, including the review of the Public Procurement Law and the law on public cemeteries. In 2021, 94,591 female and 103,108 male citizens raised their concerns to the government via the CSC in 19 districts. This participation led to the incorporation of 885 out of 33,099 citizen priorities into district plans for the fiscal year 2021/2022. Additionally, 2,622 community issues were resolved through joint actions by the community and government. Subsequently, In 2023, PPIMA partners facilitated the participation of over 240,000 citizens in decision-making fora, leading to numerous commitments from local government authorities to address the concerns raised by citizens.
During the outcome harvesting data collection process, citizens reported increased awareness and knowledge about their rights and responsibilities. This has empowered citizens to become more engaging and proactive, in particular in the CSC process. Citizens have become more informed and engaged in discussions about issues affecting them, such as the need for roads, childcare centers, and health facilities.
Due to capacity building through PPIMA in general, and community scorecard in particular, the local leaders mindset and behaviors have evolved and are now more collaborative and are open to receive citizens concerns. Similarly, local leaders are favoring a bottom-up approach compared to top-down alternative to citizens participation. As a result of PPIMA, decentralized entities work closely with citizens to solve citizens issues. Multiple examples were revealed where local authorities contributed money while citizens contributed labour. For example, in Burera districts, one of the PPIMA partners Tubibe Amahoro, in collaboration with Governance Focal Persons (GFPs), advocated for and facilitated the construction of three water runoff channels and three reservoirs. These measures redirected floodwaters away from settlements and farming lands, reducing the impact of floods and ensuring safer conditions for the local community.
Under the social protection program, the government of Rwanda has been running GIRINKA one cow per family. However numerous reports have always cited unfairness where well-to-do-families were the beneficiaries rather than the most vulnerable. PPIMA through the community scorecard raised this issue and the community advocated for the beneficiaries to be selected publicly in community gathering in order to increase transparency and mitigate injustice.
PPIMA partners have engaged in advocacy aimed at changing policies and laws to respond to citizens concerns. In 2023, in response to widespread public outcry regarding high tax rates, CLADHO in partnership with PPIMA partner CSOs, successfully advocated for the total revision of the property tax law in Rwanda. Indeed, the newly enacted Law No. 48/2023 introduced significantly reduced tax rates, lowering the cost per square meter of residential land from RWF 300 to a maximum of RWF 80. Additionally, the law abolished land transfer fees for citizens selling land, alleviating financial burdens and promoting equity among property owners and increased the prospects of people registering land transfers, keeping the system up to date.
Human Rights Awareness and Access to Justice
Transparency International Rwanda successfully advocated for the protection of whistleblowers as a necessary pillar of the integrity system in Rwanda, which culminated in the passage of a law in July 2023. This initiative strengthens protections for whistleblowers in both public and private sectors. This law provides safeguards against retaliation for individuals who report corruption, promoting a culture of accountability and transparency within Rwandan society.
Transparency International Rwanda provided vital legal aid, mediation, and advocacy services to 5,204 citizens, comprising 49% females and 51% males. Out of the 5,246 complaints received, an impressive 5,103 (97%) were successfully resolved, with 544 closed through advocacy and 572 through mediation. This initiative aimed to improve access to justice and promote alternative dispute resolution (ADR) mechanisms, significantly reducing the burden on formal legal structures across various districts, including Musanze, Rubavu, Rusizi, Huye, Kayonza, and Kigali. In addition, Transparency International Rwanda supported the establishment of 472 Citizens Concerned Committees (CCCs) across 11 districts. These committees provided ADR services, assisting 836 citizens with legal advice and referrals to legal aid services. Strengthening ADR at the community level has contributed to free and affordable access to basic legal support, empowering local communities to address disputes effectively and contribute to conflict resolution.
Another means of alternative dispute resolution is Advocacy and Legal Advice Centers (ALACs) who (together with CCCs) have facilitated access to justice for thousands of citizens, resolving community and domestic conflicts through mediation. These advocacy initiatives not only reduced burden on formal justice systems and observed backlog in the justice system but also fostered social cohesion through constructive and peaceful conflict handling. More concretely, through PPIMA- supported initiatives, 5,655 citizens (2,695 female and 2,960 male) accessed justice services, and 5,707 complaints were registered and resolved. Additionally, 505 cases of community and domestic conflicts were handled through mediation.
A citizen feedback platform for reporting corruption anonymously was launched in 2023 by Transparency International Rwanda in collaboration with the Ombudsmans Office. The platform has received 1,573 reports so far, enabling citizens to report corruption without fear of retaliation. As a pillar of integrity system in Rwanda, this initiative has enhanced citizen participation in anti-corruption efforts and increased the accountability ecosystem of public officials, fostering a more transparent public service environment.
Efforts to reduce the high rate of school dropouts among Historically Marginalized People (HMP, Twa population) in Rutsiro District have shown significant progress. The Community Scorecard (CSC) process highlighted the issue, leading to increased capacity and advocacy from HMP community volunteers. As a result, local leaders have mobilized resources to support 24 students' return to primary and secondary schools and 69 students, including teenage mothers, to join Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) for tailoring courses. This initiative has improved educational access and retention among HMP youths.
Gender Sensitive Policy, Planning and Budgeting
A significant result in this area is the work of Transparency International Rwanda who conducted research and avocacy that exposed sexual corruption in education and employment (sextorsion) which ultimately convinced parliamentarians to amend the GBV law. CLADHO presented the findings from its Budget Framework Paper (BFP) analysis to the Rwandan Parliament in 2023 which significantly influenced the budget discussions. The government committed to allocate resources to 85% of the citizen priorities identified by Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) and CLADHO during pre-budget hearings. This outcome marked a substantial advancement towards citizen-centered governance, ensuring that budget allocations aligned closely with public needs and concerns. Additionally, CLADHO's advocacy during the pre-budget hearings in 2023 successfully led to the identification and inclusion of 83% of unresolved Community Scorecard (CSC) issues in district plans and budgets across nine PPIMA districts. This significant achievement ensured that citizen concerns previously raised through the CSC were addressed in the planning process, resulting in improved public services and accountability.
Through its pre-budget and Imihigo hearings in 2023, CLADHO enabled citizen participation in formulating district budgets across nine PPIMA districts. This participatory process allowed citizens to voice 271 service delivery issues, with district authorities committing to address the majority of these concerns in the 2023/2024 fiscal year budget. By fostering engagement between citizens and local authorities, CLADHO strengthened democratic governance and ensured that local government budgets reflected the actual needs and priorities of the communities they serve.
Through the efforts of PPIMA partner CSOs, there has been a notable increase in local leaders advocating for gender equality in their communities. This outcome is significant as it plays a crucial role in achieving inclusive and equitable development by addressing power imbalances. In 2021, a total of 1,311 female and 553 male local leaders received training on women's leadership and gender equality. These trainings equipped leaders with essential skills and knowledge, enabling them to advocate effectively for gender equality and work towards reducing discrimination within their communities. This initiative demonstrates a concerted effort to empower purposively selected individuals who can influence positive change.
Environment and Climate Change awareness
Partners in PPIMA increased the advocacy capacity to influence policymakers, which led to 2.5 billion RWF in investments for sustainable water catchment restoration in drought-prone areas.
The introduction of clean cookstoves in 2500 households in Rustsiro and Burera districts led to alternative cooking methods which reduced the tree-cutting for firewood, as a mitigation measure and part of climate change adaptation. This initiative contributed to forest conservation and minimized indoor air pollution. By promoting energy-efficient cooking practices, RCCDN advanced both environmental sustainability and improved health outcomes for community members.
Through PPIMA, 1200 farmers in six districts adopted climate resilient agriculture methods, which increased the crop yield and reduced the soil degradation. related to this effort, the Women in Climate Leadership initiative supported 220 women entrepreneurs in developing climate-smart business, including solar energy distribution and organic farming.
The PPIMA project supported its partner Rwanda Climate Change and Development Network in the planting of 50,000 trees and the construction of radical terraces in the Muhanga district. These efforts enhanced environmental conservation in degraded areas and contributed to improved soil health, increased resilience to erosion, and broader environmental protection in a region prone to land degradation.
Through the support of PPIMA, We Do Green enabled 1,200 farmers across six districts in Rwanda to adopt climate-resilient agricultural practices, improving crop yields and reducing soil degradation. This initiative supported community resilience to climate change and enhanced food security for vulnerable populations. In a related effort, WDGOs Women in Climate Leadership Initiative supported 220 women entrepreneurs in developing climate-smart businesses, including solar energy distribution and organic farming. These complementary initiatives promoted economic empowerment and climate adaptation within communities.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
